Runs: `bash scripts/docs.sh .../scratch/a1/docs-reference-instructions-contacts-and-coils.log` exit 0, DOCS-OK (148 pages, no warning names this page). `elixir scripts/prose.exs --review <page>` exit 0: 0 failures, 0 passive, 0 terms with no link, 0 unchecked blocks, so the script lists no place to judge. Everything under "Sentences" is from reading. Item 3 (do the steps) does not apply to a reference page. Screenshots (1280 and 390, light and dark, body class "dark" confirmed): /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/a1/shots/icc-full-{1280,390}-{light,dark}.png and segments icc-c-<width>-<theme>-NN.png. My probes: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/a1/reader-icc/r1.exs and r2.exs, run with `elixir -pa <clone>/_build/dev/lib/logex/ebin`.

FINDINGS, MOST SEVERE FIRST

1. Lines 211, 424, 442, 455, 795: the warning rows promise warnings that logex does not give.
 - Line 211 (`ote`, Warnings): "2 writes to 1 tag, if 1 of them or more is an `ote`: programs 1 to 3". A reader takes this to cover `ote x` beside `otl x`. Probe r1.exs: `xic a ote x` / `xic b otl x`, the same with `otu`, and the reversed order all compile with no warning about `x`.
 - Lines 424, 442, 455 and table row 7 (line 795): "A second coil on the pulse bit". The glossary makes `otl` and `otu` coils. Probe r2.exs: `xic a osr s1 x` / `xic b otl x` and the same with `otu` give no warning. Only `ote`, `osr` and `osf` give one. The writer's report knew this and kept "a second coil".
 - The table "A tag with 2 coils or more" (245-252) has no row for `ote` with `otl` or `otu` on 1 tag. That is the seal-in and latch mix a controls engineer asks about.
 Mend:
 - Line 211: "A second `ote` on the same tag: program 1. A coil on the same array through a tag as a subscript: program 2. A write of the full tag beside an `ote` on 1 of its bits: program 3."
 - New row after line 250: "`ote` with `otl` or `otu` on 1 tag | The program compiles, and logex gives no warning. On a false rung, the `ote` writes 0 over the 1 of the `otl`."
 - Lines 424, 442, 455, 795: "An `ote`, an `osr` or an `osf` on the pulse bit of a different one-shot: program 7. logex gives no warning for an `otl` or an `otu` on a pulse bit."

2. Lines 168-169, 183-184, 210-211, 225-226, 240-241, 405-406, 423-424, 441-442 (and 115, 124, 125, 250, 383-384, 391, 453, 455): "Wrong rungs 1 to 13", "program 4" and "configuration 8" are plain text.
 - A reader who arrives at `#otl` from the first table reads "Wrong rungs 1 to 12 and 14 to 18" and has no link to follow. The diagnostics are 15 screens further down at 1280 px and about 25 on a phone.
 - Mend, least: make each a link, `[Wrong rungs 1 to 12](#the-diagnostics)` and `[program 4](#programs-that-get-a-warning)`.
 - Mend, better: split the output into the 5 groups it already prints, 1 heading of level 3 for each ("Wrong rungs 1 to 12: the operands", and so on), so each row links to its group. This needs 5 small scripts, or 1 script for each heading.
 - The rows are also not complete. Probe r1.exs: `xic a ton t 100 xic b ote x` and `... ons s1 ote x` give the message of wrong rung 18 for `xic b` and `ons s1`. The rows of `xic`, `xio` (168, 183) and `ons`, `osr`, `osf` (405, 423, 441) must add 18.

3. Lines 564-587 and 676-688: the 10 declarations are only inside the Elixir script.
 - The diagnostics say "`speed` is a dint (declared on line 8)", "`delay` is a ton (declared on line 9)", "`lamps` is an array of 4 bools". The page says the wrong rungs come after "the same 10 declarations" and then says "It is not necessary to read the script".
 - A controls engineer who does not read Elixir cannot tell what `speed`, `delay`, `status`, `lamps` and `boxes` are.
 - Mend: show the 10 declarations as a separate `text` block straight after line 567, before "The script". Best is a file under `examples/instructions-contacts-and-coils/` with a `file:` mark that the script reads, which also makes the script shorter. Do the same for warnings if the scripts are split.

4. Lines 62, 360, 365, 382, 388-390, 444, 452: "run" as a noun is never defined, and it carries the hardest rule of the page.
 - "the power in of its last run", "in each run", "the first run of the instance", "1 run of each one-shot". The glossary has no term `run`.
 - The difference between the last run and the last scan is the point of the rows "A rung that does not run" and "A one-shot in a function block". I went back 2 times here.
 - Mend, after line 60: "A run of an instruction is 1 time that a scan does the instruction. In most programs, each instruction has 1 run in each scan. The 2 cases of this table are the exceptions."
 - Then line 62 becomes: "An instruction has no run while its rung does not run."

5. Phone width (390 px): 4 tables are wider than the 350 px column. They scroll sideways, and the first column or the column that matters goes out of view.
 - "Form of the operand" (line 81), 612 px. The reader sees "A contact reads it" and half of "A coil writes it". "Storage bit" and "Pulse bit" are off the screen with no cue. Mend: 2 tables with the same first column, 1 for "A contact reads it / A coil writes it" and 1 for "Storage bit / Pulse bit". Make the first column the example as code (`lamp`, `lamps[2]`, `lamps[slot]`, `status.3`, `status.[slot]`, `delay.dn`, `delay.acc.3`, `s1.run`) and put the words for each form in a list before the tables.
 - The one-shot table (line 368), 696 px. Only "Power in, `s` before, Power out of `ons s`" show. The `osr` and `osf` columns are off the screen. Mend: short headings (`s` before | `ons` out | `osr`: `p` | `osf`: `p` | `s` after) and the first sentence "In the table, the first column is the power in."
 - The contacts table (line 148), 462 px. The `xio` column is cut, and it is the column that differs. Mend: headings "`xic` out" and "`xio` out".
 - The faults table (line 134), 407 px. The fault name is cut. Mend: move the cause into a sentence and keep 2 columns, Operand and Fault.
 - The console block of the diagnostics (668-779) is 700 px. Each message is cut at about 40 characters and the block scrolls as 1 piece. If finding 2's split is done, each block is short enough to scroll. If not, wrap at 56 characters.
 - The 2 timing diagrams are 599 and 584 px. They scroll inside their paragraph and show scans 1 to 4 only. This is a rule of the site, the same on each page. The table after each diagram gives the facts, so nothing is lost. Tell the owner of scripts/site.exs or the picture style: `max-width: 100%` for a page's picture is the mend. I changed nothing.
 - At 1280 px, each table fits. The 4 pictures draw in both themes, on a white card in the dark theme, and can be read. No picture says nothing.

6. Line 252 and the heading at 243: the restart rule is hard to find.
 - "A restart: the tag gets its initial value again" is the last row of "A tag with 2 coils or more". A controls engineer from Logix expects a latched bit to stay 1 through a power cycle, and looks for this under `otl`. The row "On the first scan" of `otl` (223) says only "The same as on each other scan".
 - The heading also covers "A contact after a coil" and "A restart", which are not about 2 coils.
 - Mend: put the rule in the `otl` and `otu` tables as a row "After a restart": "The tag has its initial value. A tag with the qualifier `retain` has its last value after a warm restart." Rename the heading "The value of a tag that coils write".
 - On the writer's question 4, for the reader: the rule under `otl` is enough for a reference. The comparison with Logix belongs on the explanation page for restarts, with a link from this row.

7. Lines 161, 176, 203, 218, 233, 398, 416, 434: the "Drawing" row is a sentence that describes a symbol.
 - "2 vertical lines with a diagonal line across them, and the operand over them". The real drawing is 1 to 6 screens away, and the row has no link to it.
 - Mend: `docs/examples-and-pictures.md` lets a mark draw some rungs (`<!-- rung: instructions-contacts-and-coils/eye.ld 2 -->`, a different file name). Put the 1-rung drawing under each instruction's table (eye.ld rungs 1 to 4, edges.ld rungs 1 to 3) and keep the words as its alt text. If 7 more pictures are too many, link the row: "[The drawing of `eye.ld`](#an-example-of-contacts-and-coils), rung 2".

8. Sentences that stop the reader (the checker passes each).
 - 58-59: "A true rung at an instruction is a power in that is true. A false rung at an instruction is a power in that is false." A rung is not a power. Write: "For an instruction, the rung is a true rung if its power in is true. The rung is a false rung if its power in is false."
 - 67: "the `cal` of the instance is on a false rung". `cal` is not introduced. Write: "The instruction is in a function block, and the `cal` instruction that runs the instance is on a false rung."
 - 66: "A jump goes across the rung." This is a new phrase for the glossary's "does not run the rungs between them". Write: "The rung is between a `jmp` that jumps and its label."
 - 100-101: "A storage bit and a pulse bit name the same bit in each scan." Write: "A storage bit must be the same bit in each scan. A pulse bit must be the same bit in each scan also. Thus each subscript and each bit number in its name is a literal."
 - 110-111: "A contact reads a tag that the state does not hold as 0." Read first as "does not hold as 0". Write: "If the state does not hold a tag, a contact reads the tag as 0."
 - 247, 248, 350: "The last coil ... gives the value", "The coil on the later rung gives the value", "The later rung gives the value." This is the house manner's "gives" with a subject that is not a person or logex. Write: "After the scan, the tag has the value that the last coil wrote." and "The tag has the value that the coil on the later rung wrote."
 - 252: a colon that joins 2 clauses. Write: "A tag with the qualifier `retain` keeps its value in a warm restart."
 - 226, 241: "An `ote` on the same array, if 1 of the 2 coils has a tag as a subscript: program 2". Program 2 has 2 `ote` instructions and no `otl`. Write: "An `ote` that writes an element of the same array, if 1 of the 2 coils has a tag as a subscript. Program 2 shows this warning with 2 `ote` instructions."
 - 360 and 389: "keeps" is 1 word for 2 things: stores ("keeps the power in of its last run in a storage bit") and does not change ("keeps its storage bit and its pulse bit"). Write 360 as: "The storage bit of a one-shot holds the power in of its last run: 1 for true and 0 for false."
 - 388: "The edit adds a one-shot, or it changes the rung of a one-shot. That one-shot gives no pulse..." The first sentence reads as what each edit does. Write (22 words): "If an edit adds a one-shot or changes the rung of a one-shot, that one-shot gives no pulse in its first run after the edit."
 - 390: 4 sentences with 3 ideas, the hardest cell of the page. Write: "The rule of the first scan applies only to the first scan of the program. If `cal` runs the instance for the first time in a later scan, a one-shot in the instance can give a pulse in that run. An `ons` or an `osr` gives a pulse if its rung is true. An `osf` gives a pulse if its rung is false and its storage bit has the initial value 1."
 - 391: "The one-shot sees its rung only when the task runs." "sees" is a metaphor, taken from the message. Write: "The one-shot runs only when the task runs. Thus it does not find a change of its rung that starts and ends between 2 runs of the task."
 - 444-445: "The run of an `osf` on a false rung finds the falling edge." The subject is abstract. Write: "An `osf` gives its pulse in its first run on a false rung after a run on a true rung. If the rung does not run while the power in is false, the `osf` gives no pulse."
 - 572-573: "It is not necessary to read the script... It divides a long message..." The second "It" is the script and the first is not. Write: "The script divides a long message into lines of 80 characters or fewer."
 - 18-19, first table: Kind "One-shot and coil". The page's own word is "pulse coil". Write "Pulse coil" with its glossary link.
 - No group of 4 nouns found. No missing article in prose; the fragments are in table cells only.

9. The glossary and the page say different things for 3 words the page links.
 - `storage bit` and `pulse bit`: the glossary says "The bool tag". Line 81-90 lets them be an element (`lamps[2]`) or a bit (`status.3`). Write in the glossary: "The bool in which..." and "The bool that...".
 - `rising edge` and the new `falling edge`: the glossary says "A change of a bool from 0 to 1". Lines 361-363 define the edge on the power in, which is true or false, not a bool tag. Write: "A change of the power flow to an instruction from false to true between 2 runs of the instruction. For a bool: a change from 0 to 1."
 - `one-shot`: "An instruction that is true for 1 scan when its input changes". The page says a one-shot gives a pulse, and `osr` and `osf` pass their power in. Write: "An instruction that gives 1 pulse, 1 scan long, when the power flow to it changes".

10. The order under "One-shots" and under "Coils".
 - "Rules for the 3 one-shots" comes before `ons`, but "The pulse bit" (447) comes after `osf`, though the tables of `osr` and `osf` use its rules. Move "The pulse bit" to straight after "Rules for the 3 one-shots".
 - "An example of contacts and coils" (258) sits under "## Coils". A reader of the contents takes it for a coil topic. Give the 2 examples a separate heading of level 2 ("Examples") after "One-shots", or name it under both.

11. Kind: the page is a reference almost everywhere. No history, no decision number, no plan label. The passages of a different kind:
 - Lines 105-106, "A coil on the member `r` resets the counter or the timer: `xic clear_pb ote boxes.r`. logex has no `res` instruction.", and line 454, "`xic clear_pb osr s1 boxes.r` resets the counter `boxes` for 1 scan." These are recipes. The rule (which members a coil can write) stays. The recipe goes to the how-to guide for counters and to "Instructions: timers and counters". "logex has no `res`" goes to "What logex does not have". 1 sentence with a link is enough here.
 - Lines 290-322 and 489-512: 2 Elixir scripts that differ in the file name and the inputs. They are host code that the controls engineer cannot read and the Elixir developer does not need for a rule. The suite needs them, so they stay. Add before each the sentence the page already uses for the other 2 scripts: "It is not necessary to read the script. The table after it gives the same values." The 4 scripts make the page 29,400 px tall at 1280 and 41,300 px at 390, about 200 lines of Elixir.
 - The tables "What the scan shows" (342-350, 532-541) are a worked example, which the template lets a reference have. Keep them.

12. Empathy, smaller.
 - The page says "logex gives a warning" 9 times and never says where a host finds it. Add 1 sentence at line 41: "A program that compiles holds its warnings in the field `warnings`, and `Logex.Diagnostic.format/1` gives the text of each." The scripts show this, but only in Elixir.
 - Lines 139-140: "An instruction that has such a fault writes nothing and passes no power. The scan then runs the next instruction." The reader then asks what a major fault does to a plant. Faults is a stub. Add: "[Faults](faults.md) gives what a major fault does to a plant."
 - Lines 550-551: "To find a message, search this page for its first words." This is good help, but the output wraps each message at 80 characters. A search for words copied from a terminal fails where they cross a line end. Say so: "Search for 3 or 4 words only, because the page shows a long message on 2 lines or more."
 - Line 96-97: `can go in each place that has "Yes"`. On a phone the "Yes" cells are off the screen (finding 5).

WHAT THE PAGE DOES WELL (keep it)
- The first screen: who the page is for, 1 table of the 8 instructions with a link to each, and a table of where each other rule is.
- Each instruction has the same 10 rows in the same sequence, and the 3 case tables (contacts, coils, one-shots) give each case in a line. The callout "A false rung is not a rung that does not run" comes before the rules that need it.
- Each example is shown 4 ways: text, drawing, run values and timing diagram, with a table that says what each scan shows. Each diagnostic and warning is real output with the rung that causes it.

TRUTH REVIEW: guides/reference/instructions-contacts-and-coils.md (reference), as it stands uncommitted in land2-a1 (branch doc2-a1 at 59dd1ac).

Verdict: the page's behaviour rules, values, outputs and pictures hold against the code. No example, output, picture or link is wrong. The findings are 4 warning claims that are wider than the code (1 medium, 3 of the same root), 1 place rule that forbids a legal rung, and completeness gaps. Nothing in land2-a1 was changed; no mix command ran there. All runs were in a copy (now removed) and in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/a1/truth-icc-probes/ (a.exs to i.exs, run with ./run.sh <file>; run.sh now reads land2-a1's _build ebin, read only). Logs: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/a1/truth-icc-logs/.

FINDINGS, most severe first

F1 (medium, false statement). Line 211, the `ote` row "Warnings": "2 writes to 1 tag, if 1 of them or more is an `ote`: programs 1 to 3".
Command: ./run.sh e.exs, part "2 writes to a plain tag". Output (the unused-tag warning of the probe's own `s1` removed):
  ote+otl -> no warning; otl+ote -> no warning; ote+otu -> no warning
  ote lamps[2]+otl lamps[2] -> no warning; ote c1.r+otl c1.r -> no warning
  ote+ote -> line 12: warning: `x` already has an `ote` on line 11: the last one in the scan decides it
The code (lib/logex/warnings.ex, second_otes/3: "`ote`, `osr` and `osf` are one set of coils here") does not count a latch as a second coil on the same tag. An `ote` beside an `otl` or an `otu` on 1 tag compiles with no warning. The table "A tag with 2 coils or more" (lines 245-252) has rows for `ote`+`ote` and `otl`+`otu` and no row for `ote`+`otl`, so the reader gets the wrong answer from line 211.
Correction: line 211: "A second `ote` on the same tag: program 1. An `ote` and a different coil on 1 array, if 1 of the 2 has a tag as a subscript: program 2. An `ote` on a bit and a write of the full tag: program 3." New row after line 250: "`ote` and `otl`, or `ote` and `otu`, on 1 tag | The program compiles, and logex gives no warning. The last coil that writes in the scan gives the value."

F2 (medium-low, false for `otl` and `otu`). Lines 455, 424, 442 and 795: "A second coil on the pulse bit ... logex gives a warning" / "A second coil writes the pulse bit of an `osr` or of an `osf`."
Command: ./run.sh e.exs, part "pulse bit". Output:
  osr p1 + ote p1 -> line 12: warning: `p1` is already the pulse bit of the `osr` on line 11 ...
  osr p1 + otl p1 -> no warning
  osr p1 + otu p1 -> no warning
  otl p1 then osr p1 -> no warning
  osr p1 + osf p1 -> warning; osr p1 + osr p1 -> warning; ote p1 then osr p1 -> line 12: warning: `p1` already has an `ote` on line 11
  osr status.3 + move status -> warning
The writer saw this (his third difference) and kept "a second coil". The page defines `otl` and `otu` as coils, so the sentence is false as written.
Correction: "A second `ote`, `osr` or `osf` on the pulse bit | The program compiles, and logex gives a warning. Program 7 shows the warning. An `otl` or an `otu` on the pulse bit gives no warning." Line 795: "An `ote` writes the pulse bit of an `osr` or of an `osf`." Rows 424 and 442: "An `ote` or a second pulse coil on the pulse bit: program 7."

F3 (low, wider than the code). Line 790, case 2: "A coil writes an element with a tag as a subscript, and a second coil writes an element of the same array."
Output (e.exs): otl lamps[n]+otl lamps[2] -> no warning; otl lamps[n]+otu lamps[2] -> no warning; ote lamps[n]+otl lamps[2] -> warning; otl lamps[n]+ote lamps[2] -> warning; otl lamps[2]+ote lamps[n] -> warning.
The rows of `otl` and `otu` (lines 226, 241) say it right ("An `ote` on the same array, if 1 of the 2 coils has a tag as a subscript"). Correction for line 790: "2 coils write elements of 1 array, 1 of them is an `ote`, and 1 of them has a tag as a subscript."

F4 (low, wider than the code). Line 791, case 3: "A coil writes a bit of a tag, and a different instruction writes the full tag."
Output (e.exs): move status+ote status.3 -> warning; ote status.3+move status -> warning; move status+otl status.3 -> no warning; move status+otu status.3 -> no warning.
Correction: "An `ote` writes a bit of a tag, and a different instruction writes the full tag." (README 1317-1318 says "a coil"; the code is the truth, as the writer's fourth difference says. The page's case table still says "a coil".)

F5 (low, the rule forbids a legal rung). Line 125: "After a timer instruction or a counter instruction | No instruction of this page comes after it on its rung or on its leg."
Command: ./run.sh c.exs, part "after timers/counters". Output:
  OK  "xic eye ( ton t1 100 | ote lamp )"
  OK  "( xic eye ton t1 100 | xic eye ote lamp )"
  ERR "( xic eye ton t1 100 | xic eye ) ote lamp": `ote lamp` follows `ton t1` on its path ...
An instruction in a later leg of the same branch comes after the timer on its rung and compiles. The rule is the path. It holds for `ton`, `tof`, `tp`, `rto`, `ctu` and `ctd` (each run, each refused with its own message).
Correction: "No instruction comes after it on its path: the rest of its leg and the instructions after the branch that holds it. An instruction in a different leg of the same branch is not after it. Wrong rung 18 shows the diagnostic." Also: wrong rung 18 applies to all 8 instructions (`xic lamp`, `ons s1` and `osr s1 p1` after a `ctu` are each refused), and the Diagnostics rows of `xic`, `xio`, `ons`, `osr` and `osf` do not list 18.

F6 (low, a case the first table lacks). Lines 52-56, "The power in": no row for an instruction that comes after a branch. Run (c.exs, "branch legs"): `( xic a ote x | xic b ote y ) ote z` gives z=1 if 1 leg or more passes power, z=0 if none. Correction, a fourth row: "The instruction comes after a branch. | True if 1 leg or more of the branch passes power".

F7 (low, completeness: things the code has and the page lacks).
 a. No wrong rung shows a write to a member of an instance of a function block that you write. Row 90 says "No"; the message is absent. Run (g.exs): "`ote` writes `e1.in`, but `e1` is an instance of `edge`, whose members only its body writes" (the same words for `otl`, `ons` as storage bit and `osr` as pulse bit). A contact on a `var` of the block: "`e1.s1` is not a member of `e1`, an instance of `edge`: its members are ...".
 b. Lines 102-104 name `ctu`, `ctd`, `ctud` and `rto` only. Run (h.exs): `r` is also a writable member of `ctu_int`, `ctu_dint`, `ctu_lint`, `ctu_udint`, `ctu_ulint`, each `ctud_*` and `rto_ltime`; `ld` of each `ctd_*` and each `ctud_*`. Correction: "and each typed counter and the long timer of the same kind".
 c. README 1311 ("a coil writes it and leaves every other bit") is on no reference page (grep "other bit" in guides/reference: nothing). Run (a.exs, "ote bit"): w=512 then `ote w.[3]` gives 520. Correction, in the row of line 86 or as a bullet: "A coil on a bit changes that bit only."
 d. README 336 ("A tag an instruction writes may be a `var_external`: the write is to its global, which a configuration refuses where that global is an input point") is weaker on the page: line 96 says a `var_external` "can go in each place that has Yes" with no limit. declarations-and-types.md line 189 has the rule. Correction: add "A configuration refuses a write to a `var_external` if its global is at an input point" with a link to Declarations and types.
 e. README 3031-3036 (a global that is the storage bit of a one-shot and that 2 instances write through `var_external`: a configuration warning, "the one-shot fires on the wrong scans") is not on the page. Not run by me. It is a configuration warning; if it is to stay on Warnings only, the row "1 storage bit for 1 one-shot" (line 383) could say so in 1 sentence.

F8 (low, a limit weaker in the rule row than in README). Line 391, the event-task row: "The one-shot sees its rung only when the task runs." README 2076-2078 and 3857-3861 add: "the pulse it sets stays on until the task next runs" and "a rung that is the task's trigger is true at every run, so that `xic estop osr s1 pressed` under the e-stop's own event task never pulses". The 2 facts are on the page only inside the warning text of configuration 8 (lines 902-916). Correction for the row: "A change that comes and goes between 2 runs of the task gives no pulse. A pulse bit that is 1 stays 1 until the next run of the task. A rung that is the trigger of the task is true at each run, and thus it gives no pulse."

F9 (nit, words). Line 90 uses `s1.run` for a member of a function block instance; in every other place of the page `s1` is a storage bit (`var s1 bool`). A different name, for example `seal_1.run`, removes the clash.

Item 6: no decision number, plan item, "provisional" or history on the page (grep for decision, provisional, RV-, M<n>-<n>, OE-, since, formerly, no longer: only "until" in present-tense rules).

results.result:
TRUTH REVIEW: guides/explanation/programs-as-data.md (explanation), not committed, read in a copy of land2-a2. Nothing changed in the clone; the copy is removed. Probes kept in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/a2/truth-pad-probes/ (p1.exs to p8.exs, each run with `mix run <probe>` from the copy's examples/; mut-*.log; six.log).

Verdict: the page's claims about logex hold. No statement about logex is false. 6 findings, none high: 1 statement about the Elixir compiler is too wide, 2 figures are the best case of what I measured, the rest are wording.

FINDINGS, most severe first

F1 (medium). Line 234, the table cell "If the compile raises, the BEAM does not have the old module after that." True only for an error that the compiler finds in the module's body. For an error of syntax, the most usual error in a new text, the old module stays and runs.
Command: `mix run p5.exs` (Elixir 1.20.4; `Code.compile_string` of `PadOld` again after a good compile):
```
body raises: compile -> RuntimeError; is_loaded -> false; PadOld.speed() -> UndefinedFunctionError
syntax error (missing end): compile -> MismatchedDelimiterError; is_loaded -> {:file, []}; PadOld.speed() -> 1200
token error: compile -> SyntaxError; is_loaded -> {:file, []}; PadOld.speed() -> 1200
undefined variable (compile error): compile -> CompileError; is_loaded -> false; PadOld.speed() -> UndefinedFunctionError
undefined local function in def: compile -> CompileError; is_loaded -> false; PadOld.speed() -> UndefinedFunctionError
```
The record (docs/organisation.md §4.9, "Elixir purges a module whose compilation raises") has the same wide wording, so the page copied it faithfully; the code says otherwise.
Words the page could use: "If the error is in the body of the module, the BEAM does not have the old module after that. If the error is in the syntax, the old module stays."

F2 (medium-low). Line 201, "2,000 rungs of 2 instructions each | About 0.5 ms". 0.5 ms is the least of the program shapes I tried; the writer's probe (probe_g.exs) measured a program with no output and no rung that is true. The page's own `lamps` text at 2,000 names costs about 1.1 ms.
Command: `mix run p3b.exs` (one VM; the same run gave motor.ld 2.1 µs and a compile 75.6 µs, equal to the page's figures, so the machine was comparable). {least, median} µs a scan:
```
writer's probe: var, xic a ote b / xic b otl a, all false: after-1-scan {475.4, 598.5}
var, xio n ote n (the page's lamps, as var): {728.4, 804.8}
var_output, xio n ote n (the page's lamps): {1059.7, 1149.3}
var_output, xic n ote n (all false): {780.1, 904.3}
var_input, 1 var_output: xic n ote out: {485.1, 494.8}
```
Words: "About 0.5 ms to 1 ms", or name the program: "2,000 rungs of 2 instructions each, with no output | About 0.5 ms".

F3 (medium-low). Lines 202-209: the 2 array figures are for `int`, and the prose after them says "A scan checks each element of each array" with no word that the cost depends on the type. README's unit said "an integer array's element by one guard"; the page drops that limit. An array of another type costs up to 20 times as much.
Command: `mix run p7.exs`, a 1-rung program whose state holds `<type>[65536]`, {least, median} µs a scan:
```
bool {327, 389}   int {363, 411}   dint {394, 760}   uint {464, 515}   word {904, 988}
lword {2139, 2384}   ulint {2199, 2300}   lint {3435, 5089}   lreal {4825, 5241}   real {8399, 8769}
```
Words: after the table, "These 2 figures are for an array of `int`. An array of `real` of the same size costs about 20 times as much."
Also line 202, "About 20 µs" for `int[4096]`: I measured 24.3 to 27.5 µs least, 24 to 51 µs median (p3.exs, p3b.exs); the writer's own log says 48.15. "About 25 µs" is nearer. Line 203, "About 0.4 ms": 0.34 to 0.44 ms here, right.

F4 (low). Line 231, "About 4 ms for a module with 1 function." Measured in p5.exs: a new module each time {4557, 5025} µs; the same module compiled again, which is the case of a change to a program that runs, {6972, 7478} µs. Words: "About 5 ms for a module with 1 function, and about 7 ms to compile the same module again." The logex figure, "About 75 µs for `motor.ld`", is right for `Logex.compile/2` on the text (75.6 to 89 µs); `Logex.compile_file/1`, which the page's script uses, took 247 to 262 µs with the read of the file.

F5 (low, wording that reads false). Lines 15-16 and the flowchart's label (line 116): "The Elixir compiler has no part in a compile of logex". Read literally, "a compile of logex" is the build of logex itself, which the Elixir compiler does. Words: "The Elixir compiler has no part when logex compiles a text, runs a program or makes an online edit"; label "logex compiles the text".

F6 (low, the words). (a) Lines 178 and 186: "Online edit" names a value here (the `%Logex.Edit{}` that `accept/3` returns: "An online edit reads the old one and the new one"). The glossary's online edit is the change itself ("A change to the program of an instance ... while it runs"). Words: "Edit | `Logex.Edit.accept/3` | ..." and "`Logex.Edit` reads the old one and the new one". (b) Lines 11-13 and the new glossary entry "interpret": "reads each instruction of each rung and does its operation". A scan that takes a `jmp` does not run the rungs it skips. The glossary's "scan" already has the same simplification; if the entry stays, "each rung that the scan runs" is exact. (c) Line 179: the retained image row names only `Logex.Runtime.retained/2`; a resource's image comes from `retained/1` (the glossary entry covers both). (d) Line 89: "The first 10 lines that the script prints are rung 1": line 1 is the heading `rung 1 of motor:`, the data is lines 2 to 10.

results.label: truth:explanation/scan-cycle-and-time
results.result:
TRUTH REVIEW: guides/explanation/scan-cycle-and-time.md and its 2 split pages (how-a-timer-counts-time.md, rungs-that-do-not-run.md), uncommitted in land2-a2 (HEAD 5030212)

Verdict: no statement of an example, an output, a picture or a number is wrong. 2 statements are false as written (F1, F2) and 6 are loose or weaker than the record (F3 to F8). Nothing in land2-a2 was changed (status and the 3 pages compared equal before I removed my copy).

FINDINGS, most severe first

F1 (medium). scan-cycle-and-time.md line 181, row "Cycle": "Each scan of the cycle gets the same time and the same values of the inputs."
The time is right. The inputs are not, in the glossary's meaning of "input" (a `var_input` tag, whose value "the host or a configuration gives"). A `var_input` connected to a global that an earlier instance of the same cycle wrote gets the new value in that cycle.
Probe (p6.exs, c/chain.logex: `first.a in1`, `first.x mid`, `second.a mid`, `second.x out1`, both programs `xic a ote x`):
  R.cycle(rt, 0, %{"in1" => 1}) -> {%{"out1" => 1}, [{:ran, :none, "first", 0}, {:ran, :none, "second", 0}]}
`second` read in cycle 1 the `mid` that `first` wrote in cycle 1.
Correction: "Each scan of the cycle gets the same time. The values that the host gives for the input points do not change during the cycle. An instance reads a global that an earlier instance of the same cycle wrote."

F2 (medium). scan-cycle-and-time.md line 155 "This rule is for the first scan of the instance only." and rungs-that-do-not-run.md line 41, row "A counter or a one-shot whose first run is after the first scan ... At its first run, it finds a rising edge if its rung is true."
True for a jump and for a `cal` (probed, see the list below). False for an instruction that an online edit adds: its first run finds no rising edge.
Probe (p5.exs: program v1 `xic a ote x`, 2 scans with a=1; v2 adds `xic a ons s ote pulse` and `xic a ctu c 9`; Logex.Edit.accept, then test):
  blocked after test: ["c.cu", "s"]
  first run of the added ons and ctu, a held 1: %{"n" => 0, "pulse" => 0}
  next scan: %{"n" => 0, "pulse" => 0}
Correction, page 1: "This rule is for the first scan of the instance. An online edit has the same rule for a counter or a one-shot that it adds." (with a link to online-edit-model.md). Page 3, row at line 41: start the row with "After a jump or a `cal` with no power:", or add "An instruction that an online edit adds finds no rising edge at its first run."

F3 (low to medium). scan-cycle-and-time.md lines 38 to 52 and 97 to 101. The page names the file `lamps.ld` only (the mark `<!-- file: scan-cycle-and-time/lamps.ld -->` is a comment the reader does not see), and the script reads "scan-cycle-and-time/lamps.ld". A reader who saves the file as the page names it gets a failure.
Probe (lamps.ld beside the script, `mix run scan-cycle-and-time.exs`):
  ** (MatchError) ... message: "cannot be read: no such file or directory", file: "scan-cycle-and-time/lamps.ld"
Correction: "The program `lamps.ld` is in the directory `scan-cycle-and-time` of the project." (short-pulses.md of this track has the same form, lines 52, 67, 94.) Also line 97: "The scripts of this page" is 1 script: "The script runs in the project of ...".

F4 (low). scan-cycle-and-time.md line 182, row "Round": "1 cycle, between a read of the inputs from the devices and a write of the outputs". A round reads no device. Logex.Runner's moduledoc: "Each device reads its adapter every poll period", passes on each change, and "The runner merges a change into the next round's inputs". The page's own example (reported at 22 ms, read at 30 ms) depends on this.
Correction: "1 cycle. Before the cycle, the runner takes the newest values that the devices gave for the inputs. After the cycle, it writes the outputs to the devices."

F5 (low). rungs-that-do-not-run.md line 39, row "A timer": "If its rung is true when a scan runs it again, it adds the full time since its last run." True only for a timer that was in operation at its last run; the page's line 12 says it correctly. A timer at rest starts and adds nothing.
Probe (p7.exs, jog.ld: manual, then automatic with jog_pb pressed during the jump, then manual at 3000 ms):
  now=3000 manual=1 jog_pb=1 acc=0 ...   now=3500 ... acc=500
Correction: "If the timer was in operation at its last run and its rung is true when a scan runs it again, it adds the full time since its last run."

F6 (low, the ledger: weaker than README). how-a-timer-counts-time.md lines 137 to 139: "Examples are a `move`, a comparison, an `add` and a `sub`." README (line 942 onward in the clone; 993 to 998 at 0793a86) gives the full list: "`move`, a conversion, a comparison, `add` or `sub`". The list is complete, not examples, and the page omits the conversion.
Probe (p3.exs, p2.exs): `dint_to_lint 1500 t.pre` -> "warning: `dint_to_lint` writes `1500` into `t.pre`, where `t.pre` is a ton_ltime's time in nanoseconds: 1500 ns is no whole number of milliseconds ..."; `mul t.acc 1500000 n` -> no warning.
Correction: "These instructions give the warning: `move`, a conversion, a comparison, `add` and `sub`."

F7 (low, glossary words).

TRUTH REVIEW — guides/reference/instructions-timers-and-counters.md (land2-a1, not committed; nothing changed there, no mix run there)

Verdict: the page holds up. Every check passes, every shown block is held, and about 200 statements run against logex agree with it. I found 3 statements that the code or the record contradicts, and 7 lesser items. None is a wrong value in an example or a wrong message.

Probes: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/a1/truth-itc-probes/ (h.exs, p1.exs to p10.exs, the logs). `run.sh pN.exs` there runs a probe with `elixir -pa` on land2-a1's built beams (no mix). The copy of the clone is removed.

## Findings, most severe first

**1. Lines 20, 119, 605: "on 2 rungs" is a rule the code does not have.**
The page says a `ctu` and a `ctd` of a `ctud` counter are "on 2 rungs". Both compile with no warning on 1 rung, in 2 legs of a branch, and run.
- Command: `run.sh p8.exs`
- Output: `xic eye ( ctu stock 3 | ctd stock 3 )` gives `{:ok, []}`; `( xic up ctu stock 3 | xic eye ctd stock 3 )` gives `{:ok, []}`, and its run gives `stock.cv` 0, 1, 0 for `up`, then `eye`.
- README says "on two rungs" too; the code is the truth.
- Correction: "1 `ctu` and 1 `ctd` run it. They are on 2 rungs, or in 2 legs of 1 branch." Line 605 the same; line 20 "A `ctu` and a `ctd` run a `ctud` counter."

**2. Lines 253 and 256: the range of `acc` is wrong for a run that measures no time.**
The page says, "the same for the 4 instructions", that the instruction keeps `acc` from 0 to `pre` and reads a value above `pre` as `pre`. A `tof` at rest, an `rto` on a false rung and a `tp` on a true rung with no pulse keep the value a rung wrote.
- Command: `run.sh p7.exs`, part "acc beyond pre while not timing" (`move 1000` into `acc`, preset 30).
- Output: scans 2 and 3 give `f.acc` 1000 for the `tof` at rest, and `u.acc` 1000 with `u.dn` 0 for the `rto` on a false rung; scans 7 and 8 give `u.acc` 1000 again.
- Code: `delayed(false, …)`, `retained(false, false, …)` and `pulse(false, false, timer, {true, now}, …)` in lib/logex/runtime.ex copy `acc` with no limit.
- Correction, line 253: "In a run that measures time, the instruction keeps `acc` from 0 to `pre`." Line 256: add "A `tof` at rest, an `rto` on a false rung and a `tp` with no pulse on a true rung do not change `acc`: it keeps the value that the rung wrote until the timer measures time again."

**3. Line 527: "A counter of a Logix controller does" says more than the record.**
- docs/naming.md line 864 (`ctu` stanza): "Whether the ladder CTU rolls over at the limit, as its function-block CTUD does, or stops: `unverified`." Line 894 has the rollover only for the function-block CTUD.
- README (0793a86 lines 730-731) says "where the conventional set's CTUD rolls over".
- Correction: "The up-down counter of the conventional set, the function block CTUD, does." Do not say it of every counter.

**4. Line 180: "The host gives each scan a time in ms: the third argument of `Logex.Runtime.scan/3`."**
The argument is the time since the last scan, not a clock time: `def scan(program, state, elapsed_ms \\ 0)`, and `now + elapsed!(elapsed_ms)`. A reader who passes 500, then 1000, gets 1500 ms.
- Correction: "The host gives each scan the time since the last scan, in ms: the third argument of `Logex.Runtime.scan/3`. With no third argument, the time is 0."

**5. Line 104 "until a restart" disagrees with line 202.**
A warm restart of an instance with `retain` keeps a written `pre`.
- Command: `run.sh p3.exs`
- Output: qualifier `retain`, mode warm: `t.pre=77` and `c.pv=9` before and after the restart (presets 100 and 3).
- Correction: "…until a restart that puts the preset back ([Restarts and online edits](#restarts-and-online-edits))."

**6. Line 234 (and the `rto` row, line 378): `tt` is 1 "while the rung is true and `dn` is 0" is false for an `rto` during a reset.**

result.title: A timer and a counter
result.summary: A tutorial for an Elixir developer who did "Your first program". The reader writes delay.ld (a lamp after go stays on for 3 s, with a one-shot pulse) and runs delay.exs, then writes boxes.ld (a box counter on a conveyor, lamp at 3, reset button) and runs boxes.exs. Each step shows the file, a ladder drawing, the output and a table that reads the run. It shows that the host gives the time through scan/3 and that scan/2 gives 0 ms. A timing diagram for each program. Written in place of the stub, not committed.

VERDICT: no statement of behaviour on the page is false of the code. Every value, count, message and output I ran is right. 7 findings, none blocking: 2 sentences that say more than the code does, 1 glossary word used for another thing, 4 small points.

FINDINGS, most severe first

1. Line 347, row `the last two writes:` — "The first write has the outputs of the last round." The values are those of the last round, but the last round did not make the write. Line 322 has just told the reader "If an output changed, the runner writes the outputs to the device", so the reader takes the sentence to mean the round at 32 ms wrote.
   Command: `mix run probe1.exs` (1 ms steps, `length(Sim.writes(panel))` after each):
   `e now=29 rounds=30 writes=5 ...` / `e now=30 rounds=31 writes=7 ... out=%{"panel.q.0" => 0, "panel.q.4" => 1}` / `e now=31 rounds=32 writes=7` / `e now=32 rounds=33 writes=7`.
   The write `%{"panel.q.0" => 0, "panel.q.4" => 1}` is the round's at 30 ms; the rounds at 31 and 32 ms wrote nothing.
   Words the page could use: "The first write is the write of the round at 30 ms, when `k1` changed to 0. The rounds at 31 ms and 32 ms changed no output, and thus the runner wrote nothing. `Logex.Runner.stop/1` does the second write. It writes 0 to each output."

2. Lines 196-197 — "If you see these 6 lines, the 3 files are correct." The script proves only that the 3 files compile and that the 6 globals are at their points. A wrong rung that compiles prints the same 6 lines.
   Command: in conveyor.ld change `xio stop xio fault` to `xic stop xio fault`, then `mix run first-plant-check.exs`: the 6 lines, unchanged (with that file the motor never starts in Step 4).
   Words: "If you see these 6 lines, logex compiled the 3 files, and each global is at its point." Step 4's "If you see these 12 lines, the plant runs" is the real check of the rungs, and is right.

3. Line 366 (See also) — "the same 2 tasks for your plant". "task" is a glossary word (a schedule for program instances), and this plant has exactly 2 tasks, `fast` and `main`; here the word means 2 pieces of work (write the file, run the plant). A reader takes it for `fast` and `main`.
   Words: "[Write a configuration file] and [Run a plant on the clock]: how to do each of the 2 for your plant, with the clock of the machine."

4. Lines 154 and 315 — "address" has 2 meanings on the page. Line 154: "The number is the address" (the `7` of `panel.i.7`, which is `Logex.IO.Point`'s `address`, `[7]`). Line 315: "The address is the text of the configuration file, for example `"panel.i.0"`" (the whole text, as `Logex.IO.Sim.set/3`'s doc and the glossary's `located global` use it). Both are in the code's own docs; the page should keep 1.
   Words for line 315: "It sets 1 input of the device. Give the point as the configuration file writes it, for example `"panel.i.0"`."

5. Line 321 — "In each round, the runner takes the inputs from the device". True in the glossary's sense (`round`), but the device is not read in each round: the adapter's read is at the open and at each poll of 10 ms; between them the device reports each change.
   Command: `mix run probe1.exs`: `reads after start: 1`; `reads=1` from 1 to 9 ms, `reads=2` at 10 ms, `reads=3` at 20 ms, `reads=4` at 30 ms, in 33 rounds. Also `pb_start_1 straight after set: 0` and `estop straight after set at 22: 0`: a reported change is in the plant's values only after the next round (the writer's own nuance; the page claims nothing against it).
   Words, if the sentence is kept exact: "In each round, the runner takes the newest inputs that the device gave, and runs the tasks that are due."

6. Lines 201-204, the callout — the diagnostic is shown as the script's output and nothing compares it. Mutation in the copy: `pb_start_1` changed to `pb_start_2` inside the quoted message, `mix test test/logex/readme_test.exs --only page:guides/tutorials/first-plant.md`: exit 0. Today it is exact: with `c1.start pb_start` on line 13, `mix run first-plant-check.exs` prints ``packing.logex: line 13: no global `pb_start` — did you mean `pb_start_1`?``. A change of that message will not turn the page red. Also, "An error in 1 of the 3 files gives a diagnostic" is 2 lines for an error in a `.ld` file: `xic estopp otl fault` gives ``packing.logex: line 12: program type `conveyor` does not compile: its mistakes follow, cited in `conveyor.ld` `` and ``./conveyor.ld: line 8: `estopp` is not declared — did you mean `estop`?``; and 1 diagnostic has a column (`packing.logex: line 2, column 35: ...`). Words: "An error in 1 of the 3 files gives 1 or more diagnostics."

7. Line 107, alt text — "estop latches fault" uses the glossary word "fault" for the tag `fault` (the review mode of prose.exs lists it). The alt text cannot hold code font. Words: "Rung 1: estop latches the tag fault. Rung 2: reset unlatches it. Rung 3: start or motor, and not stop, and not the tag fault, sets motor."

NOT A DEFECT, FOR THE WRITER TO WEIGH (the page says nothing false here)

results.result:
TRUTH REVIEW: guides/howto/write-a-device-adapter.md (and the new guides/howto/test-a-device-adapter.md the writer split from it)

Verdict: no statement on either page is false as written against a run, but 2 statements are too weak to keep a reader safe (F1, F2), 3 are imprecise (F3-F5), and the tables lack a few forms the code gives (F6-F8). No history, decision number, plan item or "provisional" on either page. All checks exit 0.

Where the evidence is: probes in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/b2/truth-wda-probes/ (run with `./run.sh <probe>.exs` from that directory; run.sh now points at land2-b2's build, read only); logs in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/b2/truth-wda-logs/. The copy of the clone is removed. Nothing in land2-b2 was changed and no mix command ran there.

## Findings, most severe first

F1 (medium) write-a-device-adapter.md line 203-205 and 207-210. "Give each wait in a callback a limit of time that is less than the limit of the runner." This is not enough: the limit is for the whole callback, not for each wait.
- Command: `./run.sh w.exs` (first form, kept in my first run) and `./run.sh i.exs`.
- Output: "2 waits of 300 ms in 1 read (each under 510, sum 600)": `{700, %{status: :tripped, trip: {:io, "panel", :timeout}, unzeroed: ["panel"]}, false}` (device process dead), `calls: %{read: 1}`, `at stop: []` (no 0 written, no close/1). Also `read takes 600 ms once (defaults)`: tripped after 510 ms, `:timeout`, `unzeroed: ["panel"]`. A read of 300 ms every time does not trip.
- LineDevice.read/1 itself has 2 waits in 1 callback (connect 1000 ms, then recv 1000 ms).
- What the run of the example on the real clock shows (`./run.sh silent.exs`, LineDevice unchanged, default options, a card that stops answering): `silent card: tripped after ms: {505, %{status: :tripped, trip: {:io, "panel", :timeout}, unzeroed: ["panel"]}}`, then `the card's outputs after the trip: %{0 => 1, 4 => 0}` and `the card told the controller left: false`. The motor output stays on at the card. The page says only "use a shorter wait" and does not say this result.
- Words the page could use: "Make sure that each callback returns in less time than the limit of the runner. If a callback has 2 waits, for example a connect and a receive, the limit is for their sum." and, after "LineDevice waits 1000 ms for the card": "With the default options on the real clock, a card that does not answer trips the runner with `:timeout` after 510 ms. logex stops the process of the device, and the output points of the card stay as they were."
- This supports option A of the writer's question 2 (shorter waits in line_device.exs), or at least the sentence above.

F2 (medium) line 21-26 (second Warning), line 300 and line 304. The page ties `unzeroed` to `:timeout` only. `unzeroed` also names the device when write/2 itself fails, because the 0 of the trip goes through write/2.
- Command: `./run.sh h.exs`.
- Output: `== write gives {:error, :wet, state}`: `%{status: :tripped, trip: {:io, "panel", {:error, :wet}}, unzeroed: ["panel"]}`; same for `write raises` and `write gives :ok` (wrong form). At stop logex tries the 0 one more time, then close/1: `at stop: [{:write, %{[0] => 0, [4] => 0}}, {:close}]`. A process linked in init/3 that dies gives `trip: {:io, "panel", {:down, :helper_gone}}, unzeroed: ["panel"]` (`./run.sh g.exs`).
- README (L10 area, "Not a full guarantee of outputs off") says each trip leaves "every output that can still be written at 0"; the page says less.
- Words the page could use, after the table of "When the plant runs": "If `unzeroed:` in the status names the device, logex did not write 0 to its output points: `write/2` had a failure, or logex stopped the process of the device." And in the second Warning: "The same applies if `write/2` has a failure, or if the computer or the Erlang VM stops."

F3 (low-medium) line 301, column "What to do": "Return only the addresses that `init/3` gets." init/3 also gets the output points, and an output's address from read/1 trips.
- Command: `./run.sh h.exs`. Output: `== read gives [4] => 1 (an output's address only)`: `trip: {:io, "panel", {:unknown_address, "panel.i.4"}}`.
- Words: "Return only the addresses of the input points that `init/3` gets."

F4 (low-medium) line 207-208. "For `init/3`, it is the option `open:`, 5000 ms by default." `open:` is the limit for init/3 and the first read/1 together, and for the read/1 of a restart. The start table (line 292) says the first part correctly; step 5 does not.
- Command: `./run.sh c.exs`: init 2000 ms + first read 2000 ms: `{{:ok, #PID<...>}, 4003}`; init 3000 ms + first read 3000 ms: `{{:error, {:io_init, "panel", :timeout}}, 5002}`; first read hangs: `{:io_init, "panel", :timeout}` after 5002 ms. `./run.sh r2.exs`: `restart whose read takes 700 ms: {:ok, 701}`, status running (700 ms is more than 510 ms).
- Words: "For `init/3` and the first `read/1` together, and for the `read/1` of a restart, the limit is the option `open:`, 5000 ms by default."

F5 (low) line 173-176. "In each interval, logex calls `write/2` again with the last values. Thus the device gets a write from its master in each interval". True only while the plant runs. After a trip logex writes 0 one time and then writes nothing until a restart; read/1 continues.
- Command: `./run.sh k.exs`. Output: `calls at the trip: [{:read}, {:write, %{[0] => 0, [4] => 0}}]`, `calls in 30 ms while tripped: [{:read}, {:read}, {:read}]`.
- Why it matters to the reader: hardware with a watchdog for its master sees a silent master after each trip.
- Words: "While the plant runs, logex calls `write/2` again in each interval with the last values. After a trip, logex writes 0 one time and then calls only `read/1` until a restart."

F6 (low, completeness) line 298-304. The code gives 3 forms of `trip:` that the table lacks, and line 292 says this table "gives its other forms":
- `{:io, "panel", {:thrown, term}}` and `{:io, "panel", {:exited, term}}` (`./run.sh h.exs`: `{:thrown, :ball}`, `{:exited, :gone}`). An exit is common: a GenServer.call inside a callback to a process that is down. Row 303 says only "A callback raised an exception."
- `{:io, "panel", {:down, reason}}` with `unzeroed: ["panel"]`: a process that init/3 linked stopped (`./run.sh g.exs`).
- Words for row 303: "`{:raised, message}`, `{:thrown, term}` or `{:exited, term}` | A callback raised an exception, did a throw or did an exit." A new row: "`{:io, "panel", {:down, reason}}` | A process that the adapter linked to the process of the device stopped. | Monitor that process, do not link it, if the device can continue without it."

F7 (low) line 283-292.
- The lead sentence "For a wrong adapter, `Logex.Runner.start_link/1` raises an `ArgumentError`" is not true for row 4, which is a return value (`./run.sh c.exs`: `{:error, {:io_init, "panel", :nope}}`, no exception, no EXIT message in the host). Words: "For a wrong adapter or wrong options, start_link/1 raises an ArgumentError. For a device that does not open, it returns an error."
- 2 errors about the adapter are on neither this page nor the linked table of map-io-points.md: `the device `panel`'s adapter options are a keyword list, got: :x` and `is bound to ...: an adapter is a module that implements Logex.IO, or {module, options}` (`./run.sh a.exs`, last line; lib/logex/io.ex `unlisted/2`, `adapter/3`). A reader who gives the options as a map gets the first one. Add 2 rows.

F8 (low, completeness) line 164-176 (step 4). The page gives the type of a value for read/1 but not for write/2. A real output point gets a float, and the 0 of a trip and of a stop is the integer 0 for every point, a real point too.
- Command: `./run.sh g.exs`. Output: last write while running `%{[0] => 37.5, [1] => 0}`; after a trip `%{[0] => 0, [1] => 0}`.
- An adapter that formats a real point as a float raises on that 0, and the output points are then not 0 (F2). Words: "Each value is an integer. For a `real` or an `lreal` point it is a float, but the 0 of a trip and of a stop is the integer 0."

F9 (low) line 84-101, the diagram.
- The first write/2 is before the first interval: at the start the calls are init, read, write (`./run.sh a.exs`: `init`, `read`, `write`). The diagram shows "write/2 again" in the loop before any write/2. Move "values of a round / write/2" above the loop, or put it in the loop.
- init/3 runs again at a restart after a `:timeout` or a `{:down, ...}` trip (`./run.sh z.exs`: calls at the restart `[:init, :read, :write, ...]`). The page does not say that init/3 can run more than 1 time. One sentence in step 2 is enough.

F10 (nit) line 58. "for example `0=1 1=0 2=0`": the card answers 16 values. README wrote `0=1 1=0 2=0 ...`. Words: "for example `0=1 1=0 2=0` and 13 more".

F11 (words, not the writer's alone) test-a-device-adapter.md title, line 5 and line 354; write page step 10. "test" in the glossary is the step of an online edit ("The verb is 'do a test'"). These pages use "do a test" for a check of an adapter. The planned title "Do a test of a plant on the manual clock" does the same, so this is a question for the plan, not a defect of the page. test-a-device-adapter.md line 11 "the outputs of the machine": the glossary's "output" is a tag of `var_output`; the committed map-io-points.md has the same sentence.

## The ledger (README 4961-5226, 376-383, 5693-5694, 5701-5704, 4120-4125, read against inv_B, inv_F, inv_G)
Every unit that belongs here is on 1 of the 2 pages. Weaker than README, quoted:
- README 5218-5219 "where a parse that raised would have tripped it `{:raised, ...}` with nothing said of the card": step 5 says "Do not raise an exception" and gives no reason. A run confirms README (`./run.sh v_raise.exs`: `trip: {:io, "panel", {:raised, "no answer: \"huh\\n\""}}`). One clause is enough: "a raise gives `{:raised, message}` and logex does not get the new `state`".
- README 5205-5207 "only those, since an address that is no point of the device is an I/O fault that trips the plant": step 3 says "Return no other address" with no consequence at that place (the consequence is in the table, line 301). Add "or the runner trips".
- README "Not a full guarantee of outputs off" ("every output that can still be written"): see F2.
Nothing of README's passage is nowhere. The README text of the passage has not changed since 0793a86.

## Checked and found right (each by a run)
- The 6 points, their order, direction, address and type; `[7]` prints as `~c"\a"`; `rack.i.2.4` gives `[2, 4]`.
- check/3 runs in the host's process before the runner starts and gets the same 3 arguments as init/3; a message raises ArgumentError with `the device `panel`'s adapter options: ...`; no device opens. init/3, read/1, write/2, close/1 run in a third process (not host, not runner).
- The 3 quoted start messages (`which is no module`, `which does not implement Logex.IO: it has no init/3, read/1 or write/2`, `whose check/3 gives a list of messages`) and their causes.
- init/3 `{:error, reason}` gives `{:error, {:io_init, "panel", reason}}`; a first read failure gives `{:io_init, "panel", {:error, reason}}`; `:timeout` after 5003 ms with the default `open:`.
- Defaults: poll 10 ms, idle 500 ms, open 5000 ms; the limit 510 ms (trips measured at 505 to 524 ms; 120 ms with idle: 100, poll: 20).
- 100 calls of read/1 and 100 of write/2 in 1 s on the real clock (gaps of 10 ms); a device with no output point gets no write/2, at a stop too.
- write/2 gets every output point (`%{[0] => 1, [4] => 0}`); read/1 may leave points out and logex keeps their last value; a bool takes 0 or 1 only (5, true, 1.0 give `:bad_value`); a real takes an integer or a float; an int refuses 7.0 and 40000.
- The 5 forms of the trip table, exact: `{:error, reason}`, `{:unknown_address, "panel.i.12"}`, `{:bad_value, "panel.i.0", 5}`, `{:raised, message}` with `which is none of Logex.IO's results`, `:timeout` with `unzeroed: ["panel"]`, device process dead, close/1 not called.
- Stop: write/2 with 0, then close/1. A stop of a tripped runner: close/1 only. A kill of the runner: 0, then close/1. No close/1 in the module: 0 only.
- report/2, the fragment's code: called for each message, `%{}` for an unknown message, the value in use at the next round; a wrong address trips. An adapter without report/2 drops the message.
- Step 9's block and the 9 `part of` blocks are whole lines of examples/line_device.exs; "lines 1 to 96", "98 to 172", "174 to 214" are right; the script on the test page is byte for byte examples/line_device.exs.
- test-a-device-adapter.md: the 9 lines of output equal a fresh run; each row of "The result"; each row of "If it does not work" (my own variants: v_noport `:econnrefused`, v_nocheck and v_blindcheck no line 1, v_noreconnect `0 => 1` in line 4 then the MatchError with `{:io_init, "panel", {:error, :closed}}`, v_noquit and v_noclose `false` in line 9, v_notake `{:unknown_address, "panel.i.1"}`); the Caution (a read of 700 ms on the manual clock trips nothing).
- Checks in my copy, all exit 0: `mix test test/logex/readme_test.exs --only page:<page>` (5 passed; 6 passed with the script run and compared), `--only reading:<page>` (5 and 5), `mix run scripts/draw.exs --check` (write page: no picture; test page: both `same`, and each alt text agrees with its .ld file), `elixir scripts/prose.exs --review` (0 failures, 1,517 and 938 words, 0 blocks unchecked, 1 mermaid block compared with nothing), `elixir scripts/site.exs stage` (113 pages), the 6 test files that read the pages (777 passed), `mix format --check-formatted`.
- Every block is held: 10 `part of`, 1 `fragment` (parsed; I ran the same code), 3 `file`, 2 `rung`, 1 script with its console output compared. Nothing is shown as output that nothing compares; the values in the prose and tables are the ones above.
- Links: each target exists and its title equals the link's words. Glossary: "socket", "output point", "input point", "test card" keep clear of the glossary's "connection", "input", "output".

## Could not check
- The Mermaid diagram as drawn (no script compares it, and I built no site: scripts/docs.sh is the other reviewer's). I checked its content against the runs only (F9).
- What the targets of the links say: install-and-run, restart-after-a-trip, io-adapters, runner, trips-and-watchdogs, safety-and-limits, test-on-the-manual-clock and run-on-the-clock are stubs in this clone, so "the rules of each callback", "why logex writes the output points again" and the like are promises of the plan, not checked text.
- Real hardware, and a connect that hangs (the loopback interface refuses at once), so LineDevice's connect wait was read from the code, not run.

## Not a defect of the page, for the maintainers
- While a device is tripped and `unzeroed`, the 0 is tried again only at a poll whose read/1 succeeds (lib/logex/runner/device.ex, `read/2`: `rewritten/1` is on the `{:ok, ...}` branch alone). `./run.sh w.exs`: read and write both fail for 2.5 s: `calls: %{read: 6, write: 1}`. Neither page claims a retry, so nothing to correct there; the reference page for I/O adapters should state it as the code has it.

Site built: `bash scripts/docs.sh .../scratch/b2/docs-howto-write-a-device-adapter.log` exit 0, DOCS-OK, 149 pages. `elixir scripts/prose.exs --review` exit 0: 0 failures, 1517 words, 0 passive, 11 terms with no link, 1 mermaid block.
Evidence: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/b2/reader-write-a-device-adapter/ (steps_1_to_7.exs; proj/ with reader1.exs, reader2.exs, reader3.exs; js/shot.js, js/probe.js). Screenshots: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-logex/f07aea59-53a1-5b8d-b560-6e6d2e330709/scratchpad/docs/scratch/b2/shots/write-a-device-adapter-{1280,390}-{light,dark}.png, the same with -partNN, and write-a-device-adapter-390-dark-diagram-x3.png.

FINDINGS, most severe first

1. HIGH. Lines 113-239: steps 1 to 7 cannot be done from the page. I made 1 file of the 9 blocks of steps 1 to 7 plus `end`, and ran it with logex by path: 7 compile errors (`undefined function asked/3` 2 times, `line/1`, `ok/1`, `socket/2`, `value/1`, `values/2`), `@connect` not set, `parsed/3` and `lost/2` not used. Line 113 says "parts of the module" and does not say that parts are missing. Line 154 shows `parsed(true, text, inputs)` with no caller: the reader cannot know what `true` is. The functions that return a failure from `read/1` and `write/2` (`asked/3`, `sent/2`, `answered/3`, `given_back/2`) are on the page nowhere, and they are the subject of step 5.
   Mend, line 113: "The blocks of steps 1 to 7 are parts of the module `LineDevice`. They are not the complete module. The attribute `@connect` and the functions `asked/3`, `socket/2`, `values/2`, `value/1`, `line/1` and `ok/1` are in the complete script. To run the example, copy the module from [Do a test of a device adapter](test-a-device-adapter.md)." In step 3, show `values/2`, the 2 clauses of `parsed/3` and `value/1` together (lines 81 to 89 of the file), or remove the block. In step 5, show `asked/3` to `given_back/2` (lines 55 to 69): they are what the step is about.

2. HIGH. Lines 258-271: the warning comes after the step that it is about. Step 9 gives the adapter to the runner. Step 10 then says "Do a test of the adapter before you connect the hardware." A reader who does the steps in sequence starts a runner on the hardware at step 9. The page also has no Warning that the program writes to the outputs of the machine (map-io-points.md line 263 and the test page line 8 have it).
   Mend: make step 9 the test ("Do the tests of [Do a test of a device adapter] with a test card.") and step 10 the option `io:` for the hardware, with this callout before step 10: "Warning. Do the tests of [Do a test of a device adapter](test-a-device-adapter.md) before you connect the adapter to the hardware. With the hardware, the program writes to the outputs of the machine."

3. HIGH. Lines 260-265: the block of step 9 is not what the reader writes. `opts = fn options -> [configuration: plant, io: ..., clock: {Manual, clock}] end` has `plant`, `Manual` and `clock`, which are not on this page. It is the helper of a script on the manual clock. It does not show the call of `start_link/1` or a result.
   Mend: a fragment with `{:ok, runner} = Logex.Runner.start_link(configuration: plant, io: %{"panel" => {LineDevice, host: {192, 168, 0, 20}, port: 4000}})`, then the result: "`Map.take(Logex.Runner.status(runner), [:status, :trip])` gives `%{status: :running, trip: nil}`." I ran `LineDevice` with the test card on the real clock (proj/reader1.exs): that is the exact output. Add 1 sentence: "The complete script also gives `clock:`, because it runs on the manual clock."

4. HIGH. Lines 201-210, the Caution of step 5 and its paragraph. 4 defects:
   a. Position. Steps 2, 3 and 4 write the calls that wait. The Caution is in step 5.
   b. The rule is not sufficient. "Give each wait in a callback a limit of time that is less than the limit of the runner": I ran an adapter whose `write/2` waits 300 ms 2 times (proj/reader2.exs). Each wait is less than 510 ms. Result: `trip: {:io, "panel", :timeout}`, `unzeroed: ["panel"]`, 512 ms after the start. `LineDevice.read/1` can connect (1000 ms) and then receive (1000 ms).
   c. 3 limits in 2 sentences ("a limit of time", "the limit of the runner", "that limit"). The reader cannot tell which limit "that limit" is.
   d. Line 209: "`LineDevice` waits 1000 ms for the card. For a plant on the real clock, use a shorter wait." The reader learns in a subordinate sentence that the example to copy breaks the rule of the Caution. "The real clock" is new on this page.
   Mend: move the Caution to the start of "Steps" (or to the end of "The callbacks"), with a table in place of lines 207-208:
   | Callback | Time limit | Default |
   | `init/3` and the first `read/1` | The option `open:` | 5000 ms |
   | Each other callback | The option `idle:` plus the option `poll:` | 510 ms |
   Caution: "Make each callback return before its time limit. The time limit is for all the waits of 1 callback together. If a callback does not return in time, the runner trips with `:timeout` and logex kills the process of the device. Then logex writes no 0 to the output points of the device, and `close/1` does not run."
   After it: "`LineDevice` does not obey this rule. It waits 1000 ms to connect and 1000 ms for each answer. The script runs on the manual clock, which does not move during a wait. In your adapter, make the sum of the waits less than 510 ms." (This agrees with the writer's question 2, option A: from the reader's side, change the file.) Link "watchdog" to the glossary here: `idle:` is the watchdog of the runner, and the page calls it "the limit of the runner".

5. MEDIUM-HIGH. Steps 1 to 9 and "The result" (lines 273-277) show no result. The template says "Show the result of the step straight after it" and "Show the output". The first thing that the reader can see is on a different page. 4 results cost little, and I ran each:
   - After step 4: "Compile the project. If a necessary callback is missing, the compiler prints a warning": `function read/1 required by behaviour Logex.IO is not implemented (in module Half)` (proj/reader3.exs).
   - After step 7 (line 242, "raises an `ArgumentError`"): show the message in a `text` block: ``the device `panel`'s adapter options: LineDevice needs host:, the card's address`` (proj/reader1.exs, `start_link/1` with `port:` only).
   - After step 9 and in "The result": `%{status: :running, trip: nil}`.
   - "The result" gives no next step. Add: "Then go to [Run a plant on the clock](run-on-the-clock.md)."

6. MEDIUM. Errors that the reader meets and that the tables (lines 287-304) do not name.
   a. The messages of `check/3` itself. Line 291 has only the wrong form of the return value. Add a row: ``the device `panel`'s adapter options:`` and your message | `check/3` found a wrong option | Correct the option in `io:`.
   b. `{:io, "panel", {:down, reason}}` with `unzeroed: ["panel"]`. A real adapter (a serial port, a library client) starts a process with a link in `init/3`. `LineDevice` does not, so the example hides the case. I ran it (proj/reader2.exs): a linked helper exits with `:serial_port_lost`; status shows `trip: {:io, "panel", {:down, :serial_port_lost}}, unzeroed: ["panel"]`; `Runner.restart(runner, :cold)` returns `:ok` and the status is `:running`. Add the row, and in step 2: "If `init/3` starts a process with a link, the end of that process stops the device and trips the runner."
   c. Line 198: "Return a `state` with which the next call can connect again." It is correct and hard. The page does not say the fact that makes it necessary: logex does not call `init/3` again after a failure. Write: "After a failure, logex does not call `init/3` again. It calls `write/2` with 0 for each output point, and `read/1` at the restart. Thus put into `state` that the socket is closed. `LineDevice` sets `socket` to `nil`, and `connected/1` opens a new socket in the next call." (The writer must check if logex also reads a device between the trip and the restart.) Also say what occurs after `:timeout` and `:down`: the restart opens the device again with `init/3` (moduledoc of `Logex.Runner`, "opening again each device that went down").
   d. Line 283: "For a wrong adapter, `start_link/1` raises an `ArgumentError`", but row 4 is a return value. With `{:ok, runner} =` the reader sees a `MatchError` (map-io-points.md line 319 says so). Write: "The first rows are the message of an `ArgumentError`. The last row is the value that `start_link/1` returns."

7. MEDIUM. "interval" is 1 word for 2 things (lines 93, 108, 174-176, 316). On this page it is the time between 2 reads of a device. The configuration file of the example, on the linked page, has `task fast interval 10`, and the glossary uses "interval" for a periodic task. The 2 values are 10 ms, which makes the error probable. The documentation of `Logex.IO` says "poll period". Mend: "poll period" on each line, in the diagram also (`loop each poll period`), with its definition before the diagram: "The poll period is the time between 2 reads of a device. It is the option `poll:` of the runner, 10 ms by default." Put the term into the glossary (the writer's question 6: yes).

8. MEDIUM. "master" (lines 24, 26, 175, 227) is not in the glossary and the Elixir developer does not know it. It is also a 4th word for logex, the runner and the adapter. The second Warning (lines 21-26) also gives only 1 of the cases: the output points get no 0 also when the computer stops or the cable breaks. "safe state" uses "state" in a second meaning (glossary: the values of 1 instance; the code: `state`).
   Write: "Make sure that the hardware of your device sets its output points to safe values when it gets no write. logex cannot write 0 to the output points in these 3 cases:" then a list: "the computer or the Erlang VM stops", "the cable breaks", "a callback of your adapter does not return before its time limit". Line 175: "Thus the device gets a write in each poll period." Line 227: "`LineDevice` tells the card that the adapter stops, then closes the socket."

9. MEDIUM. Lines 14-32: 3 callouts before "Before you start". On a phone they are 870 px, 2 screens, between the introduction and the first section. The Caution names `LineDevice` 17 lines before the page says what it is. The second Warning says "a callback", "in time" and "the process of the device" before lines 80-108 give them. Mend: keep the 2 Warnings at the top (the second as in finding 8, with no process). Move the Caution to "The example", straight after line 52.

10. MEDIUM. The tables on a phone (390 px, measured in the built site).
   a. Lines 65-72, the points: 491 px in a column of 350 px. `address` and `type` are off the screen, and the paragraph after the table (lines 74-76) is about `address`. Mend: 3 columns, `name`, Location, `address`, and 1 sentence: "The field `direction` is `:input` for `i` and `:output` for `q`. The field `type` is `:bool` for each point."
   b. Lines 298-304, the trips: 390 px in 350 px. "What to do" is cut at the right edge, "Cause" breaks at 1 or 2 words a line, and the table is 1621 px high (the table of lines 287-292 is 972 px). Each row starts with `{:io, "panel", `. Say it 1 time before the table: "The field `trip:` is `{:io, "panel", cause}`. The table gives each `cause`." Then column 1 has only `{:error, reason}`, `{:unknown_address, "panel.i.12"}`, `{:bad_value, "panel.i.0", 5}`, `{:raised, message}`, `:timeout`. Give the case `which is none of Logex.IO's results` a row of its own.
   c. Line 154: the line has 105 characters. At 1280 px the block cuts it at `inpu`, and the argument `inputs` is the subject of the bullet of lines 159-160.

11. MEDIUM. The diagram (lines 84-103). At 1280 px it draws and reads well in the 2 themes. At 390 px its text is 8 px high (font of 16 px, scale 350/708). In the dark theme the notes are rgb(184,182,182) on rgb(71,73,73), a contrast of about 4.6 to 1, at that size. The facts of the diagram are in no table. The aid: a table straight after the figure, which also answers "which callback is optional" and "which process":
   | Callback | Necessary | Process | logex calls it |
   | `check/3` | No | Of the host | In `start_link/1`, before the runner starts |
   | `init/3` | Yes | Of the device | 1 time, when the runner opens the device |
   | `read/1` | Yes | Of the device | After `init/3`, then in each poll period |
   | `write/2` | Yes | Of the device | After each round, and again in each poll period |
   | `report/2` | No | Of the device | For each message that the process gets |
   | `close/1` | No | Of the device | After the last `write/2`, when the runner stops |
   The paragraph of lines 105-109 (5 sentences) can then go, which pays for the words of findings 1 to 6. In the diagram, the note `check/3` is before the arrow "start the runner", but line 106 says that `start_link/1` calls it: write the note as `check/3, in start_link/1`.

12. LOW-MEDIUM. Sentences, each with its line and a new text.
   - 6-7 "for example an I/O card or a fieldbus": a fieldbus is not a device. "for example an I/O card or a device on a fieldbus."
   - 11-12 "The host writes each other adapter.": the host is an application (glossary), and the reader is the person. "You write each other adapter in your application."
   - 30 "Do not use the module `LineDevice` of this guide as it is.": the form "as it stands" of the house manner in other words. "Do not use the module `LineDevice` for a device with hardware before you change it."
   - 31-32 "The protocol of your device, its limits of time and the way to connect again are your work.": 3 abstract subjects. "You must write 3 things for your device: its protocol, the time limit of each wait, and the code that connects again."
   - 54 "It answers lines of text on a TCP socket.": the outputs are not there, and "channel" has no definition. "The card reads and sends lines of text on a TCP socket. A channel is 1 input or 1 output of the card. A point is a channel that the configuration file names."
   - 62 "The plant of the example has 6 points": the plant is not on this page. "The plant of the example is on [Do a test of a device adapter]. Its configuration file puts 6 points on the device `panel`."
   - 76 "Elixir prints the list `[7]` as `~c"\a"`.": give the cure. "To print it as numbers, use `inspect(address, charlists: :as_lists)`." (run: `[7]`).
   - 109 "which has no fixed time": "logex calls `report/2` when the process of the device gets a message."
   - 143-144: add an example of the map, as step 4 has: "for example `%{[7] => 0, [0] => 1}`".
   - 159: "Return no other address." gives no consequence. Add: "An address that is not an input point of the device trips the runner."
   - 244 "If your device sends each change of an input point": "If your device sends a message when an input point changes". Add after line 256: "`read/1` stays necessary. It can return `{:ok, %{}, state}`." (run: status `:running`).
   - 292 "the first `read/1` had a failure. If `reason` is `:timeout`, they were not complete in the time of `open:`.": "the first `read/1` returned a failure. The reason `:timeout` shows that the 2 callbacks took more time than `open:`."
   - 304 "A callback was not complete at the limit of the runner.": "A callback did not return before its time limit."
   - 2 words for 1 thing: "limit of time", "the limit of the runner", "the time of `open:`", "in time" (lines 24, 31, 203-208, 292, 304): write "time limit" on each line. "stops the process" (lines 25, 205, 304) and "the runner stops" (lines 212, 227): the first is a kill, after which `close/1` does not run, and the second is a stop, after which it runs. Write "kills the process".
   - The 11 terms of `--review`: 10 are parts of a linked term or of a title ("configuration file", "located global", "input point", "output point", "Restart after a trip", "Do a test", the callout "Warning") and must have no link. "state" is finding 8. "watchdog" must have its link in finding 4.

13. LOW. The kind. The page is a how-to guide and stays one. 2 passages belong on other pages: line 175, "Thus the device gets a write from its master in each interval, 100 times in 1 s by default", is the reason, which goes to explanation/trips-and-watchdogs.md ("See also" has the link). In its place the reader must have the instruction: "By default, that is 100 calls in 1 s. Thus make `write/2` fast, and make it safe to send the same values again." Lines 105-109 are rules of reference/io-adapters.md. The table of finding 11 holds what the steps use.

14. LOW. The way through. The first screen says what the page is for. It does not say that the reader must know Elixir: add to "Before you start" "You must know the behaviours and the processes of Elixir." The bullet of line 42 says line 3 again. Line 49-50 does not say where `line_device.exs` is (`examples/` in the repository).

DONE AS A READER
- This page: findings 1, 3 and 5. No step gives a wrong fact. Each message of the 2 tables that I ran is exact (`which is no module`, `which does not implement Logex.IO: it has no read/1`, `whose check/3 gives a list of messages, got: :ok`, `{:error, {:io_init, "panel", :econnrefused}}`, `{:io, "panel", {:error, :closed}}`, `{:io, "panel", :timeout}` with `unzeroed: ["panel"]`).
- Step 10, the linked page: in a new Mix project with logex by path, I put the 4 files that test-a-device-adapter.md shows and ran `mix run line_device.exs`. The 9 lines are the same as the page, and `LineDevice` is lines 1 to 96.
- Pages that the page links to and that are stubs in each clone: install-and-run.md, restart-after-a-trip.md, io-adapters.md, runner.md, trips-and-watchdogs.md. The step after a trip (line 306) depends on a stub.

WHAT THE PAGE DOES WELL
- Each step is a command for the adapter of the reader, with the part of `LineDevice` that does it, and steps 6, 7 and 8 start with their condition.
- The protocol table, the table of the 6 points and the note on `~c"\a"` give the reader the exact data that `init/3` gets before the reader writes a line.
- The 2 tables of "If it does not work" quote real messages and split the errors by the time at which the reader meets them, and the sequence diagram shows the process of each callback at desktop width in the 2 themes.
